props.title: I Want to Live!
props.initialSlug: Death row drama of a woman's fight for justice

sections.content: I Want to Live! (1958) revolutionized the prison film genre through Susan Hayward's raw, Oscar-winning portrayal of Barbara Graham, a real-life criminal executed at San Quentin. Director Robert Wise crafts a searing indictment of capital punishment that broke new ground in its unflinching depiction of death row and the gas chamber. The film's jazz score by Johnny Mandel adds a noir-tinged urgency, while Wise's documentary-style approach - influenced by his earlier work on The Set-Up (1949) - creates devastating authenticity. This marked a crucial shift from earlier prison films like Angels with Dirty Faces (1938), which often romanticized criminals or relied on melodrama.

sections.content: The impact of I Want to Live! resonated through later death row dramas like The Green Mile (1999) and Monster (2003). Wise's decision to focus on Graham's humanity rather than sensationalizing her crimes established a template for nuanced portrayals of condemned prisoners. The film's groundbreaking examination of media sensationalism surrounding executions particularly influenced later works like Dead Man Walking (1995) and Last Dance (1996). SUBHEAD: Evolution of the Prison Film Genre

While earlier prison films like The Big House (1930) focused on male inmates and prison breaks, I Want to Live! shifted attention to psychological trauma and systemic injustice. This paved the way for complex prison narratives like The Shawshank Redemption (1994) and Escape from Alcatraz (1979). The film's emphasis on journalistic detail and procedural accuracy influenced true-crime prison documentaries like Into the Abyss (2011).
